title: The Diamond Sutra (Sutra Text)
excerpt: Thus have I heard. At one time the Buddha dwelt at Shravasti, in the Jetavana Grove of the garden of Anathapindika, together with the great assembly of bhikshus, twelve hundred and fifty in all.

inline.s: Translated by the Tripitaka Master Kumarajiva of the Later Qin
Thus have I heard. At one time the Buddha dwelt at Shravasti, in the Jetavana Grove of the garden of Anathapindika, together with the great assembly of bhikshus, twelve hundred and fifty in all.

At that time, at the hour of meals, the World-Honored One, having put on his robe and taken up his bowl, entered the great city of Shravasti to beg for food. In the city, having begged in succession from door to door, he returned to his own place. When the meal was finished, he put away his robe and bowl, washed his feet, spread his seat, and sat down.

Then, in the midst of the assembly, the Elder Subhuti rose from his seat, uncovered his right shoulder, placed his right knee on the ground, and with palms joined, respectfully addressed the Buddha, saying: Rare is the World-Honored One! The Tathagata lovingly protects the bodhisattvas, and well commands them.
World-Honored One! When good men and good women arouse the mind of anuttara-samyak-sambodhi, on what should they abide? How should they subdue their minds?
The Buddha said: Good! Good! Subhuti, it is as you have said. The Tathagata lovingly protects the bodhisattvas and well commands them. Listen attentively now, and I shall speak for you.
When good men and good women arouse the mind of anuttara-samyak-sambodhi, they should thus abide, and thus subdue their minds. So be it, World-Honored One! I desire and delight to hear.

blocks.text: 3. The Great Vehicle, the True Teaching

inline.s: The Buddha told Subhuti: The bodhisattvas mahasattvas should thus subdue their minds: all the kinds of beings whatever they be — born from eggs, born from wombs, born from moisture, born by transformation, whether with form or without form, whether with thought or without thought, whether neither having thought nor not having thought — I shall cause them all to enter the nirvāṇa without remainder and be delivered. Though thus innumerable, countless, and boundless beings are delivered, in truth no being is delivered.
Why? Subhuti! If a bodhisattva has the mark of self, the mark of person, the mark of sentient beings, or the mark of a life span, he is not a bodhisattva.

Furthermore, Subhuti! A bodhisattva should give without dwelling anywhere. That is, he should give without dwelling in form, and give without dwelling in sound, smell, taste, touch, or dharmas. Subhuti! A bodhisattva should thus give, not dwelling in marks. Why? If a bodhisattva gives without dwelling in marks, the merit of his giving cannot be conceived.

Subhuti! What do you think — can the space of the eastern direction be conceived? No, World-Honored One! Subhuti! The space of the southern, western, northern directions, the four intermediate directions, above and below — can it be conceived? No, World-Honored One! Subhuti! The merit of a bodhisattva who gives without dwelling in marks is likewise inconceivable. Subhuti! A bodhisattva should only abide as taught.

blocks.text: 5. Seeing the Truth Through the Principle

inline.s: Subhuti! What do you think — can the Tathagata be seen by his body of marks? No, World-Honored One! The Tathagata cannot be seen by his body of marks. Why? The body of marks spoken of by the Tathagata is not a body of marks.
The Buddha told Subhuti: All marks are false and unreal. If one sees that all marks are no marks, then he sees the Tathagata.

Subhuti said to the Buddha: World-Honored One! Are there sentient beings who, hearing such words and phrases, will give rise to true faith? The Buddha told Subhuti: Do not speak thus. Five hundred years after the Tathagata's passing, there will be those who, observing precepts and cultivating merit, will be able to give rise to faith in these phrases, and take them to be true.

Know that such a person has not planted wholesome roots with a single Buddha, or two, three, four, or five Buddhas, but has already planted wholesome roots with countless millions of Buddhas. Whoever, hearing these phrases, gives rise in a single thought to pure faith — Subhuti, the Tathagata knows them all, sees them all, and such sentient beings obtain immeasurable merit.

Why? These sentient beings no longer have the mark of self, the mark of person, the mark of sentient beings, or the mark of a life span; they have neither the mark of dharmas, nor the mark of non-dharmas.

Why? These sentient beings, if their minds take up marks, become attached to self, person, sentient beings, and a life span. If they take up the mark of dharmas, they become attached to self, person, sentient beings, and a life span. Why? If they take up the mark of non-dharmas, they become attached to self, person, sentient beings, and a life span. Therefore one should not take up dharmas, nor should one take up non-dharmas.
For this reason, the Tathagata often says: You bhikshus, know that my teaching of Dharma is like a raft. Even dharmas must be abandoned, much more non-dharmas.

Subhuti! What do you think — did the Tathagata attain anuttara-samyak-sambodhi? Did the Tathagata speak any Dharma? Subhuti said: As I understand the meaning of the Buddha's teaching, there is no fixed dharma called anuttara-samyak-sambodhi, nor is there any fixed dharma that the Tathagata can speak.
Why? The Dharma spoken by the Tathagata cannot be taken up, cannot be spoken. It is neither dharma, nor non-dharma. Why is this? For all sages and saints differ by virtue of the unconditioned Dharma.

Subhuti! What do you think — if a person filled the three thousand great chiliocosms with the seven treasures and used them to give, would this person obtain much merit? Subhuti said: Very much, World-Honored One! Why? This merit is not the nature of merit, and therefore the Tathagata says it is much merit.

If again there is a person who, in this sutra, takes up and upholds even a four-line verse and speaks it for others, his merit surpasses that one. Why? Subhuti! All Buddhas, and the dharma of anuttara-samyak-sambodhi of all Buddhas, all arise from this sutra.
Subhuti! That which is called Buddha and Dharma is not Buddha and Dharma, and therefore is called Buddha and Dharma.

Subhuti! What do you think — can a stream-entrant have this thought: I have attained the fruit of stream-entry? Subhuti said: No, World-Honored One! Why? Stream-entrant is called entering the stream, yet there is nothing entered; not entering form, sound, smell, taste, touch, or dharmas, this is called a stream-entrant.

Subhuti! What do you think — can a once-returner have this thought: I have attained the fruit of once-returning? Subhuti said: No, World-Honored One! Why? Once-returner is called coming once more, yet in truth there is no coming, and this is called a once-returner.

Subhuti! What do you think — can a non-returner have this thought: I have attained the fruit of non-returning? Subhuti said: No, World-Honored One! Why? Non-returner is called not coming, yet in truth there is no not-coming, and therefore it is called a non-returner.

Subhuti! What do you think — can an arhat have this thought: I have attained the fruit of arhatship? Subhuti said: No, World-Honored One! Why? In truth there is no dharma called arhat. World-Honored One! If an arhat had this thought: I have attained the fruit of arhatship, then he would be attached to self, person, sentient beings, and a life span.

World-Honored One! The Buddha has said that I have attained the samādhi of non-contention, and among men am the foremost, the first arhat free of desire. World-Honored One! I do not have this thought: I am an arhat free of desire. World-Honored One! If I had this thought that I have attained the fruit of arhatship, then the World-Honored One would not have called Subhuti one who delights in the practice of a forest-dweller. Because Subhuti in truth does nothing, he is called one who delights in the practice of a forest-dweller.

blocks.text: 10. The Adornment of a Pure Land

inline.s: The Buddha told Subhuti: What do you think — when the Tathagata was formerly with Dipankara Buddha, did he obtain anything in the Dharma? No, World-Honored One! When the Tathagata was with Dipankara Buddha, in truth in the Dharma there was nothing obtained.
Subhuti! What do you think — do the bodhisattvas adorn the Buddha-lands? No, World-Honored One! Why? One who adorns the Buddha-lands does not adorn, and therefore is called adorning.

Therefore, Subhuti! All the bodhisattvas mahasattvas should thus give rise to a pure mind: they should not give rise to a mind dwelling in form, nor give rise to a mind dwelling in sound, smell, taste, touch, or dharmas; they should give rise to a mind that dwells nowhere.

Subhuti! Suppose a person had a body like Mount Sumeru, king of mountains. What do you think — is such a body great? Subhuti said: Very great, World-Honored One! Why? The Buddha speaks of a non-body, and so it is called a great body.

Subhuti! As there are as many grains of sand in the Ganges as there are, so there are as many Ganges rivers as there are sands. What do you think — are these sands of the many Ganges rivers many? Subhuti said: Very many, World-Honored One! The Ganges rivers alone are already countless, much more their sands.

Subhuti! I now tell you truthfully. If good men and good women filled three thousand great chiliocosms, as many as those sands of Ganges rivers, with the seven treasures, and used them to give, would they obtain much merit? Subhuti said: Very much, World-Honored One!
The Buddha told Subhuti: If good men and good women, in this sutra, take up and uphold even a four-line verse and speak it for others, this merit surpasses the former.

blocks.text: 12. The Honoring of the True Teaching

inline.s: Furthermore, Subhuti! Wherever this sutra is spoken, even a four-line verse of it, know that in that place all the devas, humans, and asuras of the world should make offerings, as to a Buddha-tower or a shrine. How much more so when a person is able to take up, uphold, read, and recite it entirely.
Subhuti! Know that such a person accomplishes the supreme, first, and rarest Dharma. Wherever this sutra is found, there is the Buddha, and there are his honored disciples.

At that time, Subhuti said to the Buddha: World-Honored One! What shall this sutra be named? And how shall we uphold it? The Buddha told Subhuti: This sutra is named the Diamond Prajna-Paramita. By this name you should uphold it.
Why? Subhuti! The Buddha speaks of prajna-paramita, which is not prajna-paramita, and therefore is called prajna-paramita.
Subhuti! What do you think — has the Tathagata spoken any Dharma? Subhuti said to the Buddha: World-Honored One! The Tathagata has spoken nothing.
Subhuti! What do you think — are all the atoms of dust in the three thousand great chiliocosms many? Subhuti said: Very many, World-Honored One!
Subhuti! Of the atoms of dust, the Tathagata speaks non-atoms, and therefore they are called atoms of dust. The Tathagata speaks of worlds, of non-worlds, and therefore they are called worlds.

Subhuti! What do you think — can the Tathagata be seen by the thirty-two marks? No, World-Honored One! The Tathagata cannot be seen by the thirty-two marks. Why? The thirty-two marks spoken of by the Tathagata are not marks, and therefore are called the thirty-two marks.

Subhuti! If good men and good women gave up body and life as many times as the sands of the Ganges, and if again a person, in this sutra, takes up and upholds even a four-line verse and speaks it for others, his merit would be very much greater.

blocks.text: 14. Departing From Marks, Entering Still Extinction

inline.s: At that time, Subhuti, hearing this sutra, deeply understood its meaning and, weeping with tears of sorrow, said to the Buddha: Rare is the World-Honored One! The Buddha speaks such a profound sutra. From of old, with the eye of wisdom I have never heard such a sutra.

World-Honored One! If again there is a person who, hearing this sutra, has faith in a pure mind, he then gives rise to the real mark. Know that such a person accomplishes the first and rarest merit. World-Honored One! This real mark is not a mark, and therefore the Tathagata calls it the real mark.

World-Honored One! Now that I have heard such a sutra, to believe, understand, take up, and uphold it is not difficult. But in a future time, in the last five hundred years, if sentient beings hear this sutra, believe, understand, take up, and uphold it, such a person will be the first and rarest.

Why? Such a person has no mark of self, no mark of person, no mark of sentient beings, no mark of a life span. Why is this? The mark of self is not a mark; the mark of person, the mark of sentient beings, the mark of a life span are also not marks. Why? Leaving all marks is called all the Buddhas.
The Buddha told Subhuti: So it is! So it is! If again there is a person who, hearing this sutra, is not startled, not frightened, not afraid, know that such a person is very rare.
Why? Subhuti! The Tathagata speaks of the first paramita, which is not the first paramita, and therefore is called the first paramita.
Subhuti! The paramita of patience, as spoken by the Tathagata, is not the paramita of patience, and therefore is called the paramita of patience.

Why? Subhuti! When in the past I had my body cut in pieces by King Kali, at that time I had no mark of self, no mark of person, no mark of sentient beings, no mark of a life span. Why? If, when I was dismembered limb by limb, I had the mark of self, the mark of person, the mark of sentient beings, the mark of a life span, then I would have given rise to anger and hatred.

Subhuti! I also recall that in the past, for five hundred lives, I was a patient ascetic, and in those lives I had no mark of self, no mark of person, no mark of sentient beings, no mark of a life span.
Therefore, Subhuti! A bodhisattva should depart from all marks and arouse the mind of anuttara-samyak-sambodhi.

He should not give rise to a mind dwelling in form, nor give rise to a mind dwelling in sound, smell, taste, touch, or dharmas; he should give rise to a mind that dwells nowhere. If the mind dwells anywhere, it is not truly dwelling. Therefore the Buddha says that the mind of a bodhisattva should not dwell in form when giving. Subhuti! For the sake of benefiting all sentient beings, a bodhisattva should thus give.
The Tathagata says that all marks are not marks. Again he says that all sentient beings are not sentient beings.
Subhuti! The Tathagata is a speaker of truth, a speaker of reality, a speaker of thusness, a speaker who does not deceive, a speaker who does not differ.
Subhuti! The Dharma attained by the Tathagata — this Dharma is neither real nor unreal.

Subhuti! If the mind of a bodhisattva dwells in dharmas and then gives, it is like a man entering a dark place, where he sees nothing. If the mind of the bodhisattva does not dwell in dharmas and then gives, it is like a man with eyes, in the bright light of the sun, seeing all kinds of forms.

Subhuti! In a future age, if good men and good women are able to take up, uphold, read, and recite this sutra, the Tathagata, with his Buddha-wisdom, knows them all and sees them all, and they all accomplish immeasurable and boundless merit.

blocks.text: 15. The Merit of Upholding the Sutra

inline.s: Subhuti! If good men and good women gave up their bodies as many as the sands of the Ganges in the morning, again as many such bodies in the middle of the day, and again as many such bodies in the evening, and gave up their bodies for countless hundreds of thousands of myriads of eons; and if again there is a person who, hearing this sutra, has faith without revulsion, his merit surpasses that one — how much more so one who writes it, takes up and upholds it, reads and recites it, and explains it for others.
Subhuti! In summary, this sutra has inconceivable, immeasurable, boundless merit. The Tathagata speaks it for those who arouse the great vehicle mind, for those who arouse the supreme vehicle mind.

If a person is able to take up, uphold, read, and recite it, and broadly speak of it for others, the Tathagata knows such a person and sees such a person, and they all accomplish immeasurable, unnameable, boundless, inconceivable merit. Such people are those who bear the burden of the Tathagata's anuttara-samyak-sambodhi.

Why? Subhuti! If one delights in a lesser Dharma, then, attached to views of self, views of person, views of sentient beings, views of a life span, he will not be able to hear, receive, read, or recite this sutra, nor explain it for others.

Subhuti! Wherever this sutra is found, all the devas, humans, and asuras of the world should make offerings. Know that this place is a tower, and all should bow in reverence, make offerings and circumambulate, and scatter flowers and incense about it.

Furthermore, Subhuti! If good men and good women, taking up, upholding, reading, and reciting this sutra, are despised by others, these people's karmic offenses from former lives, for which they should fall into evil paths, — because they are despised by people in this present life, their karmic offenses from former lives are thereby destroyed, and they shall attain anuttara-samyak-sambodhi.

Subhuti! I recall that in an inconceivable number of asankhya kalpas in the past, before Dipankara Buddha, I met eighty-four hundred thousand millions of nayutas of Buddhas, and to all of them I made offerings and served them, without any omission. If again there is a person who, in the last age, is able to take up, uphold, read, and recite this sutra, the merit he obtains — not one part in a hundred, not one part in a thousand myriads of millions even, up to the limits of arithmetic and parable, can equal it.

Subhuti! If good men and good women, in the last age, take up, uphold, read, and recite this sutra, the merit they obtain — if I were to speak of it in full, some who hear it would have their minds run wild and become confused, doubting and disbelieving. Subhuti! Know that the meaning of this sutra is inconceivable, and its fruit of recompense is also inconceivable.
At that time, Subhuti said to the Buddha: World-Honored One! When good men and good women arouse the mind of anuttara-samyak-sambodhi, on what should they abide? How should they subdue their minds?

The Buddha told Subhuti: Good men and good women who arouse the mind of anuttara-samyak-sambodhi should give rise to this mind: I shall deliver all sentient beings, and having delivered all sentient beings, there is in truth not a single sentient being who is delivered.
Why is this? Subhuti! There is in truth no dharma by which one arouses the mind of anuttara-samyak-sambodhi.

Subhuti! What do you think — did the Tathagata, at the place of Dipankara Buddha, have a dharma by which he attained anuttara-samyak-sambodhi? No, World-Honored One! As I understand the meaning of the Buddha's teaching, the Buddha, at the place of Dipankara Buddha, had no dharma by which he attained anuttara-samyak-sambodhi.

The Buddha said: So it is! So it is! Subhuti! There is in truth no dharma by which the Tathagata attains anuttara-samyak-sambodhi. Subhuti! If there were a dharma by which the Tathagata attains anuttara-samyak-sambodhi, then Dipankara Buddha would not have given me the prophecy: In a future life you shall become a Buddha named Śākyamuni. Because there is in truth no dharma by which one attains anuttara-samyak-sambodhi, therefore Dipankara Buddha gave me the prophecy, saying: In a future life you shall become a Buddha named Śākyamuni.
Why? The Tathagata is the meaning of the thusness of all dharmas.

If someone says that the Tathagata attains anuttara-samyak-sambodhi — Subhuti, there is in truth no dharma by which the Buddha attains anuttara-samyak-sambodhi. Subhuti! The anuttara-samyak-sambodhi attained by the Tathagata is in it neither real nor unreal.
Therefore the Tathagata says that all dharmas are the Buddha-dharma. Subhuti! That which is called all dharmas is not all dharmas, and therefore is called all dharmas.
Subhuti! It is like a person of great bodily stature. Subhuti said: World-Honored One! The Tathagata speaks of a great bodily stature, which is not a great body, and therefore is called a great body.

Subhuti! The bodhisattva is likewise. If he says, I shall deliver countless sentient beings, he is not called a bodhisattva. Why? Subhuti! There is in truth no dharma called bodhisattva. Therefore the Buddha says that in all dharmas there is no self, no person, no sentient beings, no life span.

Subhuti! If a bodhisattva says, I shall adorn the Buddha-land, he is not called a bodhisattva. Why? The Tathagata says that one who adorns the Buddha-land does not adorn, and therefore is called adorning. Subhuti! If a bodhisattva understands the dharma of no self, the Tathagata calls him a true bodhisattva.
Subhuti! What do you think — does the Tathagata have the fleshly eye? So it is, World-Honored One! The Tathagata has the fleshly eye.
Subhuti! What do you think — does the Tathagata have the heavenly eye? So it is, World-Honored One! The Tathagata has the heavenly eye.
Subhuti! What do you think — does the Tathagata have the eye of wisdom? So it is, World-Honored One! The Tathagata has the eye of wisdom.
Subhuti! What do you think — does the Tathagata have the dharma eye? So it is, World-Honored One! The Tathagata has the dharma eye.
Subhuti! What do you think — does the Tathagata have the Buddha eye? So it is, World-Honored One! The Tathagata has the Buddha eye.
Subhuti! What do you think — as to all the sands in the Ganges, does the Buddha speak of them as sand? So it is, World-Honored One! The Tathagata speaks of them as sand.

Subhuti! What do you think — if there are as many Ganges rivers as all the sands of one Ganges, and as many Buddha-worlds as the sands of all these Ganges rivers, would there be many of them? Very many, World-Honored One! The Buddha told Subhuti: In all those lands, the various minds of all the sentient beings, the Tathagata knows them all.
Why? The Tathagata says that all minds are not minds, and therefore are called minds.
Why is this? Subhuti! The past mind is unobtainable; the present mind is unobtainable; the future mind is unobtainable.

blocks.text: 19. The Universal Transformation of the Dharma-Realm

inline.s: Subhuti! What do you think — if a person filled the three thousand great chiliocosms with the seven treasures and used them to give, would this person, by this causal condition, obtain much merit? So it is, World-Honored One! This person, by this causal condition, would obtain very much merit.
Subhuti! If merit had reality, the Tathagata would not say that much merit is obtained. Because merit is without reality, the Tathagata says that much merit is obtained.

Subhuti! What do you think — can the Buddha be seen in his perfect body of form? No, World-Honored One! The Tathagata should not be seen in his perfect body of form. Why? The Tathagata says that the perfect body of form is not a perfect body of form, and therefore is called the perfect body of form.

Subhuti! What do you think — can the Tathagata be seen in his perfect marks? No, World-Honored One! The Tathagata should not be seen in his perfect marks. Why? The Tathagata says that perfect marks are not perfect, and therefore are called perfect marks.

Subhuti! Do not say that the Tathagata has this thought: I shall speak a Dharma. Do not have this thought! Why? If anyone says that the Tathagata speaks a Dharma, he slanders the Buddha, as he does not understand what I have spoken. Subhuti! One who speaks the Dharma has no dharma to speak, and therefore is called speaking the Dharma.
At that time, the wise Subhuti said to the Buddha: World-Honored One! Are there sentient beings who, in a future age, hearing this Dharma, will give rise to faith?

The Buddha said: Subhuti! They are not sentient beings, nor are they not sentient beings. Why? Subhuti! Of sentient beings, the Tathagata says they are not sentient beings, and therefore they are called sentient beings.
Subhuti said to the Buddha: World-Honored One! Did the Buddha attain anuttara-samyak-sambodhi, that which nothing is attained?
The Buddha said: So it is! So it is! Subhuti! With regard to anuttara-samyak-sambodhi, I have not even a smallest dharma that can be attained; and therefore it is called anuttara-samyak-sambodhi.

blocks.text: 23. Doing Good With a Pure Mind

inline.s: Furthermore, Subhuti! This Dharma is equal and without high or low, and therefore is called anuttara-samyak-sambodhi. By cultivating all good dharmas without self, without person, without sentient beings, without a life span, one attains anuttara-samyak-sambodhi.
Subhuti! That which is called good dharmas, the Tathagata says is not good dharmas, and therefore is called good dharmas.

Subhuti! If, in the three thousand great chiliocosms, there were mountains of all the Sumerus, king of mountains, and such great accumulations of the seven treasures, and someone held them and used them to give; while another person, with this Prajna-Paramita sutra, even a four-line verse, takes up, upholds, reads, recites, and speaks it for others, the former merit would not be one part in a hundred, not one part in a hundred thousand myriads of millions, even up to the limits of arithmetic and parable.
Subhuti! What do you think? You must not say that the Tathagata has this thought: I shall deliver sentient beings.

Subhuti! Do not have this thought. Why? In truth there are no sentient beings whom the Tathagata delivers. If there were sentient beings whom the Tathagata delivers, then the Tathagata would have self, person, sentient beings, and a life span.
Subhuti! The Tathagata speaks of self, which is not a self; yet the common people think there is a self.
Subhuti! As for the common person, the Tathagata says he is not a common person, and therefore he is called a common person.

blocks.text: 26. The Dharma-Body Is Not a Mark

inline.s: Subhuti! What do you think — can the Tathagata be contemplated by the thirty-two marks? Subhuti said: So it is! So it is! The Tathagata can be contemplated by the thirty-two marks.

The Buddha said: Subhuti! If the Tathagata could be contemplated by the thirty-two marks, then a wheel-turning sage-king would be the Tathagata. Subhuti said to the Buddha: World-Honored One! As I understand the meaning of the Buddha's teaching, the Tathagata should not be contemplated by the thirty-two marks.
Then the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
If one sees me through form, or seeks me through sound,
That person walks a perverse path, and cannot see the Tathagata.

Subhuti! If you have this thought: the Tathagata does not attain anuttara-samyak-sambodhi by reason of perfect marks. Subhuti! Do not have this thought: the Tathagata does not attain anuttara-samyak-sambodhi by reason of perfect marks.

Subhuti! If you have this thought that one who arouses the mind of anuttara-samyak-sambodhi speaks of all dharmas as cut off and extinguished, do not have this thought! Why? One who arouses the mind of anuttara-samyak-sambodhi does not speak of a mark of cutting off and extinguishing dharmas.

Subhuti! If a bodhisattva filled worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges with the seven treasures and used them to give; while another person, knowing that all dharmas are without self, attains patience — this bodhisattva's merit surpasses the former bodhisattva's. Why? Subhuti! Because all bodhisattvas do not receive merit.

Subhuti said to the Buddha: World-Honored One! How is it that the bodhisattva does not receive merit? Subhuti! In the merit a bodhisattva accomplishes, he should not covet or cling, and therefore it is said he does not receive merit.

Subhuti! If someone says that the Tathagata comes or goes, sits or lies down, this person does not understand the meaning I have spoken. Why? The Tathagata comes from nowhere and goes nowhere, and therefore is called the Tathagata.

blocks.text: 30. The Mark of a Unitary Whole

inline.s: Subhuti! If good men and good women ground the three thousand great chiliocosms into atoms of dust, what do you think — would these compounds of atoms be many? Subhuti said: Very many, World-Honored One! Why? If these compounds of atoms really existed, the Buddha would not have spoken of them as compounds of atoms. Why is this? The Buddha speaks of compounds of atoms, which are not compounds of atoms, and therefore they are called compounds of atoms.

World-Honored One! The three thousand great chiliocosms spoken of by the Tathagata are not worlds, and therefore are called worlds. Why? If a world really existed, it would be a mark of a unitary whole. The Tathagata says the mark of a unitary whole is not a mark of a unitary whole, and therefore is called the mark of a unitary whole.
Subhuti! The mark of a unitary whole is that which cannot be spoken; yet the common people covet and cling to the matter.

blocks.text: 31. Knowledge and Views Do Not Arise

inline.s: Subhuti! If someone says that the Buddha speaks the view of self, the view of person, the view of sentient beings, the view of a life span — Subhuti, what do you think — does this person understand the meaning I have spoken? No, World-Honored One! This person does not understand the meaning spoken by the Tathagata. Why? The World-Honored One says that the view of self, the view of person, the view of sentient beings, the view of a life span are not such views, and therefore are called views.
Subhuti! One who arouses the mind of anuttara-samyak-sambodhi should, with regard to all dharmas, thus know, thus see, thus believe and understand, without giving rise to a mark of dharmas.
Subhuti! That which is called the mark of dharmas, the Tathagata says is not a mark of dharmas, and therefore is called the mark of dharmas.

blocks.text: 32. The Response and Transcendence Are Not Real

inline.s: Subhuti! If someone filled worlds as countless as the asankhyas with the seven treasures and used them to give; if good men and good women who arouse the bodhi-mind uphold this sutra, even a four-line verse, taking it up, upholding it, reading and reciting it, and proclaiming it for others, their merit surpasses that one.
How should it be proclaimed for others? Without taking up marks, unmoved in thusness.
Why is this so?
All conditioned dharmas are like a dream, an illusion, a bubble, a shadow,
Like a drop of dew, like a flash of lightning—thus should they be regarded.

When the Buddha had spoken this scripture, the Elder Subhuti, together with the monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen, and all the gods, humans, and asuras of the world, having heard what the Buddha said, were filled with great joy, and with faith received and practiced it.
